title: Apps may keep giving us tools to break our addiction to them, but teens aren’t using them
summary: Guess how many teens use anti-doomscrolling features. Hint: It's NOT "practically everyone."
body: TL;DR Tools like Digital Wellbeing or Instagram’s Take a Break are built to interrupt addictive use cycles. In an ongoing Meta trial, a former data scientist shares just how few teens actually took advantage of the company’s tools. With teen accounts, Take a Break is now on by default, hopefully pushing numbers up a little. Are smartphones our best friends, or our worst enemies? Sometimes it feels like half the work companies are putting into new features are attempts to fix our addiction to others, like with the new Pause Point on Pixel 11 devices — or really anything Digital Wellbeing , for that matter. And while we seem to keep getting more and more new tools meant to save us from ourselves, are the most vulnerable people even using them? According to Meta, maybe not so much. title: Fan survey sends Google a pretty blunt message about the Pixel 12
summary: Our readers told us what the Pixel 12's focus should be, and it's not more AI.
body: Like it or not, Google has made AI a huge part of the Pixel experience, and that’s only become more obvious with the Pixel 11 series. Gemini Intelligence and other smart features were a major focus of this year’s launch — so much so that you’d assume this was what all the fans were screaming out for. It’s always quite tricky to know how true that is, so we were curious about where you think Google needs to go next with the Pixel 12. We recently asked our readers exactly that. My colleague Robert Trigg certainly has his own ideas about this direction, and made them abundantly clear in a recent article . His argument in a nutshell is that the Pixel 11 shows Google is approaching something of a hardware breaking point. He wasn’t unhappy with Google’s AI work, but pointed out that rival flagships are pushing ahead in fundamental areas such as battery capacity, charging speeds, camera hardware, and raw performance, while Pixels haven’t kept pace. With the Pixel 12 next to face that challenge, we asked you via a poll in the article whether Google should prioritize better hardware, even smarter AI, both, or simply more competitive prices.

title: Google Home automations not working right lately? Blame your TV
summary: Google Home automations aren't playing nicely with your TV, but Google is on the case.
body: TL;DR Google Home users are reporting automations tied to TV starters failing to run. Google confirms an investigation is underway into problems with TV-based automations. So far the reports we’ve seen involve TCL models, but it’s not clear if other brands are similarly impacted. If you’re looking to configure a really impressive smart home, Google Home automations are your best friend. While routines are great for pulling off complicated multi-device workflows, automations take that to the next level by, well, automating them — instead of manually activating a routine, automations begin all by themselves when their starter event occurs. At least, that’s the way things are supposed to work, but right now there’s a frustrating glitch impacting automations tied to TVs. Over on Reddit’s Google Home sub, users have been complaining about automations involving their TVs that fail to work . While you should be able to use events like powering your TV on or off to trigger an automation, Google Home just doesn’t seem to recognize when these starter events happen.

The change appears on the stable YouTube app, but it hasn’t reached every device. The new behavior could be part of a broader YouTube UI refresh. YouTube’s interface has become something of a moving target lately. The company was only recently testing a new button arrangement on Android that removed text labels from the controls under videos. And now, a small change to how YouTube shows skipped time appears to be rolling out to some Android users. The change involves YouTube’s familiar double-tap gesture for skipping. Currently, you can double-tap the right side of the screen to jump forward or the left side to rewind, while touching and holding the scrub bar lets you manually move through the video. In the current UI, double-tapping skips forward or backward without showing how much time you’ve moved. When manually scrubbing, however, YouTube displays the amount of time you’ve skipped in the video interface, as seen in the screenshot below.

This broke popular use cases for using Now Playing’s notifications to import songs into apps, such as Last.fm. What followed was dissatisfaction from users, which Google is now looking to address. It is working to add notifications for the currently playing track back to the app with a future update.

title: Chrome’s new rules ruined ad blockers. Here are 4 things that still work

body: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority A few years ago, Chrome introduced Manifest V3 and began phasing out the older Manifest V2 technology used by some of the most advanced browser extensions. title: Nintendo just went nuclear on Switch emulators (again)
summary: Nintendo just can't stand Switch games running on anything other than a Switch.
body: TL;DR Nintendo has filed seven new DMCA notices taking down over 400 GitHub repositories related to Switch emulators. The notice took down repos for emulators such as Suyu, Skyline, and several others. It’s no secret that Nintendo has historically taken an extremely strict stance against emulators and people using its IP without permission. A few months ago, the company sent DMCA notices to take down several Switch emulators whose code was hosted on GitHub. Now, the company has thrown another proverbial Donkey Kong barrel at more such GitHub repositories. Nintendo has filed seven DMCA complaints with GitHub to take down over 400 repositories related to Switch emulators in a single day (via TorrentFreak ). This includes emulators like Suyu, which gained popularity after the Yuzu emulator shut down in 2024. According to the DMCA notice displayed publicly on the Suyu repository, GitHub took down all 311 repositories in the network due to Nintendo’s DMCA notice.
